content: The document titled Pneumonia – Prevention and Control is a publication by the World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF, copyrighted in 2013. It emphasizes that the designations and content within the publication do not reflect any official stance by WHO regarding the legal status of countries, territories, or boundaries. Additionally, the mention of specific companies or products does not imply endorsement by WHO over others of a similar nature. While all reasonable precautions were taken to verify the information, the material is distributed without any warranty, and the responsibility for its interpretation and use lies with the reader. The publication introduces the Integrated Global Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Pneumonia and Diarrhoea (GAPPD), which aims to eliminate preventable deaths caused by these two diseases by 2025. Pneumonia and diarrhoea are among the leading causes of death in children under five, accounting for 29% of all deaths in this age group and resulting in the loss of approximately 2 million young lives annually. The GAPPD framework is built on three pillars: Protect, Prevent, and Treat. Protect: Establish good health practices from birth, such as exclusive breastfeeding for six months, adequate complementary feeding, and vitamin A supplementation. Prevent:g., pertussis, measles, Haemophilus influenzae type b, pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, and rotavirus), promote handwashing with soap, provide access to safe drinking water and sanitation, reduce household air pollution, and prevent HIV transmission. Treat: Improve care-seeking behavior and referral systems, manage cases at health facilities and community levels, and provide essential supplies like oral rehydration salts (ORS), zinc, antibiotics, and oxygen. Continued feeding, including breastfeeding, is also emphasized during illness. The GAPPD sets ambitious but achievable goals for 2025, including reducing pneumonia mortality in children under five to fewer than 3 per 1,000 live births, reducing diarrhoea mortality to fewer than 1 per 1,000 live births, and decreasing the incidence of severe pneumonia and diarrhoea by 75% compared to 2010 levels. Additionally, it aims to reduce global stunting in children under five by 40% compared to 2010 levels. To achieve these goals, the plan targets 90% full-dose vaccine coverage, 90% access to appropriate case management for pneumonia and diarrhoea, and at least 50% exclusive breastfeeding during the first six months of life. The document highlights the need for coordinated and integrated efforts at national and global levels, involving governments, health systems, communities, and partners. It stresses the importance of using proven interventions, such as exclusive breastfeeding, vaccination, ORS, and improved sanitation, to address the root causes of pneumonia and diarrhoea. The GAPPD also emphasizes equity, focusing on reaching the most vulnerable and underserved populations, particularly in low-resource settings where the burden of these diseases is highest. The publication acknowledges the significant progress made in child survival over the past two decades but notes that progress has been uneven across and within countries. Pneumonia and diarrhoea disproportionately affect children in the poorest regions, particularly sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, where nearly 90% of deaths occur. The burden of these diseases exacerbates existing inequalities, placing additional strain on families and health systems in low-resource settings. It underscores the need for political will, resource mobilization, and collaboration among stakeholders to achieve the ambitious targets and make preventable child deaths due to pneumonia and diarrhoea a tragedy of the past.
